title: Six Employees, Six Continents
subtitle: How a company nobody had heard of briefly changed the world's COVID policy
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, documentary narration. Calm and unhurried — the voice of something that has read the whole record and feels the weight of it without raising its voice. Clinical and precise, not outraged. Small pauses at periods. Let the plain facts carry the disbelief.
grade: Muted 2020 documentary still, clinical and quiet — hospital corridors, empty offices, laptops, archive rooms, cool blue-grey palette, fine film grain, no readable text or screens, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: May twenty-second, twenty twenty. The Lancet — one of the two most trusted medical journals on Earth — published a study of ninety-six thousand COVID patients, in six hundred seventy-one hospitals, on six continents.
beats.img: An empty hospital corridor at night, fluorescent ceiling lights, clinical and quiet, muted blue-grey tones, no readable signage, no people.

beats.vo: The largest hydroxychloroquine study ever run.

card.unit: patients — the largest hydroxychloroquine study ever run

beats.vo: The study found the drug didn't help COVID patients. It found it might be killing them. Within three days, the World Health Organization paused its own global drug trial.
beats.cap: WHO paused its own trial within 3 days
beats.img: An empty pharmacy medicine cabinet, rows of shelves in soft clinical light, muted blue-grey, no readable labels, no people.

beats.vo: All of it came from one company. A firm called Surgisphere, run by a surgeon named Sapan Desai, that claimed real-time access to the electronic health records of hospitals on every continent but Antarctica.
beats.cap: One company supplied all of it
beats.img: A closed laptop on an empty desk, a single desk lamp, muted tones, no visible screen content, no people.

beats.vo: The company's own LinkedIn page listed six employees.

card.sub: claiming a live data pipeline from 671 hospitals worldwide

beats.vo: One title was science editor. The person holding it was a science-fiction writer. Another was listed as a marketing executive. Neither journal had checked.
beats.img: A small empty corporate office suite, an empty desk with no computer, blinds half-drawn, soft daylight, muted tones, no people.

beats.vo: Two days after publication, a statistician on the other side of the world started asking simple questions the paper never answered. Which hospitals. Whose data. Why every continent looked so oddly similar.
beats.img: A desk with papers and a calculator under a soft desk lamp, muted tones, no readable text, no people.

beats.vo: Australian doctors were the ones who broke it open. The paper claimed more COVID deaths in five Australian hospitals than Australia's entire government had recorded, nationwide, on that same date.
beats.cap: More deaths than the whole country had
beats.img: A hospital records office, rows of filing cabinets under fluorescent light, muted colors, no readable labels, no people.

beats.vo: Within a week, two hundred and one scientists had signed an open letter, listing ten separate reasons the numbers simply couldn't be real.

card.unit: scientists signed an open letter within a week
card.sub: listing 10 separate reasons the numbers weren't real

beats.vo: The paper's other authors asked Surgisphere for the raw data, so an independent auditor could check it. Surgisphere said no. The data belonged to hospitals it wouldn't name, under contracts it wouldn't show anyone.
beats.img: A closed office door at the end of a dim corridor, muted tones, quiet and institutional, no readable signage, no people.

beats.vo: Thirteen days after publication, the paper was retracted. A companion paper in the New England Journal of Medicine, built on the same company's data, was pulled the very same day.
beats.img: A stack of printed journal pages on a desk, soft overhead light, muted tones, no readable text, no people.

beats.vo: We can no longer vouch, the retraction said, for the veracity of the primary data sources.

card.head: "We can no longer vouch"
card.accent: "for the veracity of the primary data sources."

beats.vo: The World Health Organization resumed its own trial the very next day. Its own independent safety board had found nothing wrong with the drug. What had been wrong, the entire time, was the data that said otherwise.
beats.cap: WHO resumed its trial the next day
beats.img: An empty hospital waiting room, rows of chairs in soft clinical light, muted blue-grey, quiet, no people.

beats.vo: One of the paper's own authors lost his university position over it. It later came out that he was related, by marriage, to the man who ran Surgisphere — and it was he who had brought the company in, in the first place.
beats.cap: The two men were related by marriage
beats.img: An empty university faculty office, a bookshelf in soft shadow, a bare desk, muted tones, no readable text, no people.

beats.vo: Thirteen days, publication to full retraction, for a study that had already reached six continents.

card.sub: for a study that had already reached six continents

beats.vo: Surgisphere's website went dark within weeks. Its social media accounts disappeared. Nobody has heard from Sapan Desai since.
beats.cap: The company went dark within weeks
beats.img: A small vacant office storefront at dusk, blinds drawn, an empty parking space out front, muted urban tones, no readable signage, no people.

beats.vo: I checked. Six years later, the company's own website still doesn't load at all.
beats.cap: I checked. It still doesn't load.
beats.img: A dim, empty small office interior seen through a window at dusk, no lights on inside, muted tones, quiet, no people.

beats.vo: Two of the most trusted medical journals in the world published it anyway. Nobody checked, because nobody thought they would ever need to.
beats.cap: Nobody thought they'd need to check
beats.img: An empty hospital waiting room corridor, rows of chairs receding into soft clinical light, muted blue-grey, no people.
